6.2 — Ground Checks: No Infinite Jumps

Your jump works. That is the problem. Tap the key in mid-air and you jump again, and again, and again — a jump with no ground check is not a jump, it is a jetpack with infinite fuel. Today you teach the script to ask a question it has never asked: am I standing on something?

The Problem: You Can Jump in Mid-Air ~10 min

Open the cave and press Play. Jump once, then keep tapping the key while you are in the air. You climb. Nothing stops you, and the Console says nothing, because from the computer's point of view your code is working exactly as written: if the key went down, add an impulse. There is no rule about where you are allowed to do that.

Your goal: a jump that only fires when the character is standing on something. So start with the honest question — how would a script ever know it is standing on something? Nothing in the Rigidbody2D says "grounded". There is no event that fires when you touch a floor and another when you leave it. You have to go and ask.

The floor is already there. The question is not. The cave's Collision tilemap already carries a TilemapCollider2D, a CompositeCollider2D and a Rigidbody2D with Gravity Scale 0, which is why your character lands on it instead of falling through. Collision already works. What does not exist yet is any code that asks about it — and that is the entire lesson.

Select the Collision tilemap in the cave and read its Inspector carefully. Note two things: it is tagged Ground (the tag already exists in this project, along with a tag called GroundCheck), and its Layer is Default. Then open Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers and scroll the Layers list. Find the empty user layer slots. A tag is a name you can compare against; a layer is a bucket the physics engine can filter on. The project has the tag and does not have the layer — and you are about to find out why that distinction costs people entire afternoons.

Socratic: Asking Versus Remembering

  1. A tag and a layer are both just names attached to an object. Why can a raycast be told to ignore everything except one layer, but not "everything except one tag"?
  2. The Collision tilemap is tagged Ground right now. If you wrote a ground check that compared tags, would it work — and what would it cost you every frame you ran it?
  3. Your character is standing still on the floor. Is "grounded" a fact you could store when you land, or a fact you should re-check every frame? What could change it without any code of yours running?
  4. Standing on the floor is not the same as standing on the floor. Should a crate, a moving platform or an enemy's head count as ground? Who decides — the physics engine or you?
  5. A jump that fires in mid-air is not a crash, an error or a warning. What does that tell you about the kind of bug this is, and how you have to find it?
Read the Docs: Four Ways to Ask About the Ground ~20 min

Every platformer ever shipped uses one of these. Read all four — the differences are in what each one can tell you and where each one lies to you.

TechniqueThe question you are askingWhat it needsWhat it returnsWhere it lies to you
Physics2D.Raycast(origin, Vector2.down, distance, mask) "Is there a ground-layer collider directly below this exact point?" An origin (usually your feet, not your centre), a distance, and a LayerMask. A RaycastHit2D: the collider, the distance to it, the exact contact point and the surface normal. It is one infinitely thin line. Stand with one pixel of your feet over the edge of a tile and it reports air.
Physics2D.OverlapCircle(point, radius, mask) "Is there a ground-layer collider anywhere inside this circle at my feet?" A point, a radius, and a LayerMask. The collider only — no direction, no distance, no contact point. A wall beside your feet is inside the circle too, so you can be "grounded" against a vertical surface.
Collider2D.IsTouchingLayers(mask) "Is my own collider touching anything on this layer, right now?" Your Collider2D and a LayerMask. No origin, no distance, no ray. A single true or false. It can only see contacts that physically exist — a Kinematic body needs Use Full Kinematic Contacts ticked or it will report false while standing on the floor.
OnCollisionStay2D(Collision2D c) with a layer or tag check "What am I in contact with during this physics step?" A callback method, plus a rule to stop it re-firing your jump every step. The whole collision: the object, the contact points, the relative velocity. It fires continuously, so a naive jump fires continuously too; and it does not fire at all for a Kinematic body against static colliders unless full kinematic contacts are enabled.
Two names from the docs that are the same idea. A LayerMask field in the Inspector looks like a dropdown, but it is an integer whose bits mark which layers you care about. That is why "Everything" is not a special case in the code — it is simply all the bits switched on, which is exactly why it is the setting that produces the classic bug in a moment.

Choose Your Check

  1. Which of the four did you pick, and which one does your character's shape argue for? A wide-footed character and a narrow one do not fail the same way.
  2. Two of the four can tell you how far the ground is. Name a game behaviour that needs that distance, and say whether your game has it.
  3. The circle check would call a wall "ground". Is that a bug you would fix, or a feature a wall-slide or wall-jump would later exploit?
  4. The collision-callback check needs no mask and no distance — it is the laziest to write. What does it demand instead, and which Rigidbody2D checkbox can silently break it?
  5. Your body type was chosen back in 2.2. Read your own answer again: does your body type rule out one of these four techniques entirely?
  6. Whichever you choose, the value you compute has to be re-derived every frame rather than stored once when you land. What is the argument for that, and what kind of object would argue the other way?
Build Lab: Create the Layer, Then Ask ~25 min

Step 1 — create the Ground layer. In Edit → Project Settings → Tags and Layers, find the first empty User Layer and name it Ground. Close the window. Note what did not happen: no object in your project changed. A layer is a name for an empty bucket until something is put in it — and layers are project-wide, not per-scene, so you do this once for the whole game.

Step 2 — put the floor in the bucket. In the cave, select the Collision tilemap and set its Layer dropdown (top right of the Inspector) to Ground. Do the same for every other solid surface you intend to land on — platforms, crates, ledges you have placed yourself. Do not do it to the No Collision tilemap: that one is decoration, and a raycast that hits it will tell you that you are standing on scenery.

Architectural specification: the check.
  • Which technique did you choose, and what are its exact inputs — origin, direction, distance, mask?
  • Where does the origin sit? The character's root is at its centre, and a ray fired from the centre has to travel through your own legs before it reaches the floor. What is the fix — an offset, a child object, or a different technique?
  • How far is "down"? Measure the real gap from your collider's bottom edge to the tile surface, then write that number down. Guessing here is what produces the bug in a moment.
  • Where does the mask come from — a serialized LayerMask field, or a hard-coded layer name? Which one lets a teammate fix your level without opening your script?
  • Where is the result stored, and what type is it? A bool named for the question ("am I grounded") reads better than one named for the technique.
  • Does the check run in Update() or FixedUpdate()? Remember that the answer is a physics answer, produced by physics, on the physics clock.
  • Is the jump condition now compound? Write the whole sentence in English before you write it in C#.
Architectural specification: making the invisible visible. Before you trust a check you cannot see, draw it. OnDrawGizmos runs in the editor and can draw a line from your origin along your check direction, scaled by your distance. Three lines of code turn "my jump doesn't work" into "my whisker is too short" in about four seconds. Draw it in one colour when the check is false and another when it is true.

Step 3 — the mask experiment. Set your mask to Everything and press Play. Stand still on the floor, then jump. If your origin sits inside your own collider, the ray hits you at distance zero and reports ground forever — the jetpack is back, and now it is wearing a disguise. This is the first bug in the project that the mask alone prevents, and it is the same reason a turret's projectile must ignore the turret that fired it. Put the mask back to Ground and confirm the check is honest again.

Step 4 — the honesty test. Watch your gizmo while you: stand still (true), jump (false the moment you leave), land (true), walk off a ledge (false). If any of those four is wrong, your distance or your origin is wrong, not your logic.

Bug Hunt: The Flying Ant ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Set your check distance to something huge — two or three tiles. You can now jump while standing on thin air near a ledge. How far from the ground does the character have to be before it stops being "grounded", and what is the honest name for the state you accidentally built?
  2. Move your origin to the character's exact centre with a short distance. What does the ray hit first, and why does the jump still work while standing but fail at the lip of a ledge?
  3. Set the mask to Everything and stand on the floor. Name every object in the cave the ray could now be hitting, and describe the symptom in one word (jetpack).
  4. Put the layer on the No Collision tilemap by mistake. Where does the character now believe it can jump from, and what does the gizmo whisker look like while it happens?
  5. If you chose OnCollisionStay2D: leave it firing the jump with no extra rule and hold the key. How many physics steps per second is it being called on, and what does your character do?
  6. If you chose IsTouchingLayers and your body is Kinematic, read the Rigidbody2D Inspector for Use Full Kinematic Contacts. With it unticked, what does the check report while you are standing still on solid floor — and where would you have looked first if you had not read this question?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Check Design

  1. Fire two checks — one at each foot — instead of one in the centre. Which single-coordinate bug does that fix, and what is the cost to your frame budget on a level with fifty characters?
  2. Draw your gizmo in a second colour when the check is false. Why does a designer who never reads your script still benefit from that?
  3. Make the check ignore the ground for a moment after a jump so you can drop through a platform. What has to be true about the platform's collider for a "drop through" to be possible at all?
  4. Your Animator already has IsWalking, WalkDir and Attack. A jump pose needs a fourth fact. Which parameter type would you add, and which single line in your ground check now earns its keep?
  5. Look at Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts/TopDown_EnemyAnimator.cs and read how it decides what to animate. It has no ground check at all — why does the top-down world not need one, and what does that say about the cave?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain the difference between a tag and a layer, with your own project as the example
  • Create a layer, assign it to the right objects, and say which objects must not get it
  • Compare the four ground-check techniques and defend your choice
  • Show the check with a gizmo and tune the distance by measurement, not by guessing
  • Explain the self-hit bug and what a LayerMask prevents
  • Explain why the grounded value is re-derived every frame instead of stored
  • Commit and push
